title: Talcum Powder Lawsuit: Lawyer Fees and Status (Oct 2026)
description: How talc lawyers are paid, J&J's proposed $5.5B ovarian deal and its 95% participation condition as of October 2026, and questions to ask before joining.
h1: How much does a talcum powder lawsuit cost, and where does it stand?
summary: Talc claimants usually pay their own lawyer a contingency percentage of any recovery plus case costs. As of October 2026, J&J's July 27, 2026 proposal to resolve about 76,000 ovarian talc claims for $5.5 billion (first payment of up to $3 billion in 2027) required at least 95% participation, and we found no public confirmation that the threshold had been met. J&J's three bankruptcy attempts were dismissed, the last on March 31, 2025.
body:
Talc litigation status as of October 2026

  • Bankruptcy attempts ended: Johnson & Johnson tried three times to resolve talc claims through subsidiary bankruptcies (LTL Management twice, then Red River Talc). All were dismissed; Red River was dismissed on March 31, 2025.[1] Ovarian cancer cases returned to the federal multidistrict litigation (MDL 2738) in New Jersey and to state courts.
  • July 22, 2026: the MDL court issued an order to show cause, cited by J&J in its announcement.[2] Insurance Journal reported that a federal judge's ruling the prior week "cast doubt" on about 69,000 cases.[3]
  • July 27, 2026, proposed deal: J&J announced a proposed resolution of about 76,000 remaining ovarian talc claims in federal and state court, with a $5.5 billion commitment; the first payment is no more than $3 billion in 2027, with no additional payments due before 2028.[2] Lead plaintiffs' counsel said the total could reach $7 billion or more and that claims would be paid within 18 months.[3]
  • 95% condition: the deal requires participation by at least 95% of the remaining claims.[2] We found no public confirmation, as of October 11, 2026, that the threshold has been met, and the announcement gives no participation deadline.[2][3]
  • Trials continue: J&J issued statements on talc verdicts through September 28, 2026, when it said a jury rejected a plaintiff's claims in the Pelley case.[4]
  • Mesothelioma claims: J&J says it previously settled about 95% of filed mesothelioma talc lawsuits; the proposed $5.5 billion deal is for ovarian claims.[2]

How talc lawyers are paid

Talc claimants generally hire lawyers individually on contingency: a percentage of any settlement or verdict, no fee if there is none. The agreement must be in writing, state the percentage at each stage, and say whether case expenses are taken before or after the fee is calculated.[5] If your case is in an MDL or a coordinated state proceeding, more of the work (experts, discovery, bellwether trials) is shared across cases, but your own agreement still decides what you pay.

Questions to ask about the proposed deal:

  • If I participate, what percentage will you take from my payment, and is it calculated before or after costs?[5]
  • Will any court-ordered common-benefit or administrative assessment be deducted, and is it taken from your fee or from my share?
  • What costs have been charged to my file so far?
  • What happens to my case, and to your fee, if I do not participate or if the 95% threshold is not met?[2]
  • When would I actually be paid, given that the first payment is scheduled for 2027?[2]

Illustrative arithmetic only (hypothetical amount, not an estimate of any claim). If a participating claimant's allocation were $60,000, the agreement set a 33⅓% fee on the gross, case costs of $3,000 were charged, and a 2% assessment of $1,200 came out of the client's share: fee $60,000 × 1/3 = $20,000; net $60,000 − $20,000 − $3,000 − $1,200 = $35,800. If the fee were calculated after costs and the assessment were absorbed by the firm: ($60,000 − $3,000) × 1/3 = $19,000; net $60,000 − $19,000 − $3,000 = $38,000.

Participating vs. staying in litigation

The proposal is a settlement offer, not a court judgment, and it depends on enough claimants agreeing. Participating trades the uncertainty of trial (and the risk raised by the July 2026 show-cause order) for a payment schedule that starts in 2027.[2] Declining keeps your case in court, where outcomes have varied and costs continue. This is a decision to make with your own lawyer, using the specific allocation and release terms they show you in writing.

If you never filed a claim, ask a lawyer promptly about your state's deadline; the general injury deadline for each state is on its state page, but product-liability and discovery rules may differ.

Red flags

  • Anyone promising a set talc payout or a guaranteed share of the $5.5 billion.
  • Pressure to sign a participation form without seeing the fee calculation and release terms.
  • Requests for up-front fees to "join" a settlement.
  • Sources that cite older bankruptcy plans as if they were still pending; the Red River case was dismissed in March 2025.[1]

faq.q: Is there a talcum powder settlement in 2026?
faq.a: There is a proposal, not a final deal. On July 27, 2026, J&J announced a $5.5 billion proposal for about 76,000 ovarian talc claims, conditioned on at least 95% participation; we found no confirmation that the threshold was met as of October 11, 2026.

faq.q: How much do talc lawyers charge?
faq.a: Usually a contingency percentage of any recovery set by your written agreement, plus repayment of case costs. Ask how fees and any common-benefit assessments would be applied to a payment under the proposed deal.

faq.q: When would talc settlement payments be made?
faq.a: Under J&J's announcement, the first payment is no more than $3 billion in 2027, with no further payments due before 2028, and only if the deal's conditions are met.

faq.q: What happened to the J&J talc bankruptcy?
faq.a: All three attempts were dismissed; the last, Red River Talc, was dismissed on March 31, 2025, and the cases returned to the court system.
